Article.ArticleTitle: Treatment of Small Peri-Implant Buccal Dehiscence Defects With SCTG or GBR: 3-Year Results of a Pilot Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: To evaluate and compare subepithelial connective tissue grafts (SCTG) and guided bone regeneration (GBR) for the treatment of small peri-implant buccal bone dehiscences over a 3-year follow-up, in terms of profilometric contour change, peri-implant parameters and patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).

Patients presenting with small buccal bone dehiscences (≤ 3 mm) after single implant placement were included. Defect sites were randomly treated with either SCTG or GBR, while five patients without dehiscences served as a negative control group. All patients received an implant crown and were followed for 3 years. Profilometric measurements, marginal bone levels, peri-implant parameters, and PROMs were recorded at baseline, 1, and 3 years. Data were analyzed descriptively.

A total of 16 patients were available for the 3-year follow-up (SCTG, n = 5; GBR, n = 6; negative control, n = 5). Both augmentation approaches maintained stable buccal soft-tissue contours. At 1 mm below the mucosal margin, the median buccal contour change was 0.19 mm (Q1: -0.28; Q3: 0.29) in the SCTG group and 0.11 mm (Q1: -0.20; Q3: 0.30) in the GBR group. At 3 mm below the mucosal margin, the corresponding median contour changes were 0.05 mm (Q1: -0.36; Q3: 0.31) for SCTG and -0.05 mm (Q1: -0.22; Q3: 0.07) for GBR. Peri-implant clinical parameters (probing depth, bleeding on probing, and plaque) remained stable, indicating maintained peri-implant health in both groups. Marginal bone levels were preserved throughout the observation period and oral health-related quality of life remained high and comparable between the SCTG and GBR groups.

Within the limitations of this pilot study, both SCTG and GBR were associated with stable buccal contour conditions and favorable peri-implant health over a 3-year follow-up period. These findings were observed under adequate self-performed plaque control and adherence to supportive care. Adequately powered RCTs are needed to confirm these findings.

Article.ArticleTitle: Pink lipoma along the ventral tongue: uncommon clinical presentation.

Abstract.AbstractText: Oral lipomas are relatively uncommon mesenchymal lesions primarily composed of mature fat cells and may be associated with a myriad of lesser-known histologic variants that contain populations of spindle cells, smooth muscle, cartilage, blood vessels, collagen, myxoid tissue, and/or salivary glands. Lesions typically arise on the buccal mucosa and exhibit a yellow to yellow-pink hue. The aim of this article is to report an unusual case of a moderately pink lipoma on the ventral tongue.

Article.ArticleTitle: How clinicians think: a qualitative exploration of perceptions and management strategies for temporomandibular disorders.

Abstract.AbstractText: this study aimed to explore the decision-making process of clinicians regarding the management of temporomandibular disorders (TMD) and analyze the experiences encountered when managing this group of conditions.

a qualitative design was adopted where semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 healthcare providers specialized in oral medicine or oral (maxillofacial) surgery. They were directed using a topic guide covering subjects such as their experiences with patients with TMD, their perceptions regarding this condition, perceived challenges, management approach and influencing factors. The discussions were audiotaped and transcribed verbatim. Thematic analysis was utilized to analyze the data.

Five themes were identified: "perceptions and views," "challenges unique to TMD," "general approach to management," "factors influencing treatment decisions," and "barriers and facilitators of a successful outcome."

Managing temporomandibular disorders remains a complex challenge for healthcare providers. This study described multiple clinician, patient, and healthcare-related obstacles to effective care. The shortage of strong evidence regarding the different management strategies further complicates treatment. While education and conservative management remain cornerstones of treatment, various factors influenced the decision-making process, such as the patients' preferences and circumstances and the clinicians' own specializations and experiences.

Article.ArticleTitle: Orofacial Cleft Characteristics in Van der Woude Syndrome: A Retrospective Study in Japan.

Abstract.AbstractText: Van der Woude syndrome (VWS) is a common syndromic cause of orofacial clefting, yet comprehensive phenotypic data in Asian populations remain limited. This retrospective study delineated the clinical characteristics and anatomical severity of VWS patients managed at Aichi Gakuin University Dental Hospital, Japan (April 1989-September 2026). Among 5528 cleft patients, 22 VWS cases were identified. The cohort demonstrated a female predilection (59.1%) and a high proportion of patients without a documented family history of orofacial clefts or lip pits (59.1%). Pathognomonic lower lip pits were highly prevalent (86.4%) and predominantly bilateral (59.1%). Cleft lip and palate (CLP) was the most frequent phenotype (59.1%), followed by cleft lip and alveolus (22.7%), submucous cleft palate (SMCP) (13.6%), and cleft lip (4.5%). All 19 overt clefts were complete. Notably, Lip-Alveolar-Palate (L-A-P) anatomical mapping revealed eight distinct morphological patterns, with bilateral complete CLP emerging as the most prevalent structural model (22.7%). This study highlights the phenotypic variability and anatomical severity of VWS among Japanese patients treated for orofacial clefts, marked by a skew toward complete CLP and an absence of overt cleft palate. Recognizing this spectrum, including subtle manifestations such as SMCP, is important for accurate diagnosis and genetic counseling, and multicenter studies with genetic testing are needed to define the full range of VWS phenotypes in Asian populations.

Article.ArticleTitle: Auranofin Sensitizes Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma to PD-1 Blockade Through DUSP1-Associated Macrophage Reprogramming.

Abstract.AbstractText: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is frequently refractory to immune checkpoint blockade, in part because the tumor microenvironment is enriched with immunosuppressive, M2-like tumor-associated macrophages. Auranofin (ARN), an FDA-approved thioredoxin reductase inhibitor, induces oxidative and proteotoxic stress and may remodel myeloid compartments to improve immunotherapy responsiveness. Here, we investigated whether ARN sensitizes OSCC to PD-1 blockade through DUSP1-associated macrophage reprogramming. Using an immunotherapy-resistant, syngeneic MOC2 murine OSCC model, mice bearing established tumors were treated with vehicle, ARN, anti-PD-1, or combination therapy. Combination treatment significantly improved survival and produced the most pronounced reduction in tumor burden compared with control and monotherapy groups. In vitro, ARN increased Dusp1 mRNA in bone marrow-derived macrophages polarized toward an M2 phenotype in a time- and dose-dependent manner. In vivo, RNAscope analysis demonstrated increased Dusp1 expression within tumors following ARN and/or anti-PD-1, with co-localization patterns consistent with a shift toward a pro-inflammatory macrophage state. Functionally, ARN directly promoted macrophage repolarization, increasing the M1/M2 ratio by flow cytometry and suppressing expression of the M2 marker arginase-1 (Arg1). In tumors, ARN and anti-PD-1 each increased the frequency of M1-like macrophages while reducing M2-like populations. Adaptive immune profiling further showed increased CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration across treatments, peaking in the combination group. Tumor cells also upregulated PD-L1, PD-L2, and CTLA-4, consistent with heightened immune stress. Collectively, these findings support repurposing ARN as an immunomodulatory adjuvant to overcome resistance to PD-1 blockade in OSCC by inducing DUSP1-linked macrophage remodeling and enhancing cytotoxic T-cell-associated antitumor immunity.
